questions.prompt: Which company currently owns and develops BlazeMeter?
questions.explanation: BlazeMeter is a Perforce product. Apache develops JMeter itself, which BlazeMeter is compatible with but does not own.

questions.prompt: Taurus (bzt) is an open-source tool that can run JMeter tests locally without a paid BlazeMeter plan.
questions.explanation: Taurus is open source and runs JMeter on your own machine. A BlazeMeter account is only needed to report to or run on BlazeMeter.

questions.prompt: In BlazeMeter, what is an engine?
options: A load generator machine provisioned for a test run
questions.explanation: Engines generate the traffic. They are not the system under test, which is why Engine Health is reported separately.

questions.prompt: Which are parts of a BlazeMeter performance test definition? Select all that apply.
options: The script and its data files
questions.explanation: A test combines script and files, load configuration and distribution, plus optional failure criteria. BlazeMeter never needs your application's source code.

questions.prompt: Your app is an intranet HR system reachable only inside the company network. You need 2,000 users. What is the most appropriate BlazeMeter option?
options: Public cloud engines pointed at the intranet host name
A private location with agents inside the network, if your plan includes it
Use the Chrome extension's Run button
questions.explanation: Cloud engines cannot reach internal hosts. A private location runs agents inside your network that only make outgoing connections to BlazeMeter. More cloud locations do not change reachability.

questions.prompt: A colleague says the free plan allows a specific number of users, quoting a 2019 blog. What should you do before planning a test?
options: Check the current plan limits on BlazeMeter's pricing page or your account billing screen
Ask on a forum and use the most common answer
questions.explanation: Plan limits change over time. The live pricing page and your account are the source of truth.

questions.prompt: Your app calls a third-party payment API on checkout. You plan a 1,000-user BlazeMeter test of your own staging environment. What must you do about the payment calls?
options: Nothing; you own the staging app
Stub or virtualise the payment API, or get the provider's written permission for load
Spread load across locations so the provider does not notice
questions.explanation: Owning your app does not authorise load on a third party's service. Stub it or get permission. Hiding traffic or timing does not change authorisation.

questions.prompt: A team asks whether to move their 50-user nightly regression JMeter test, which runs fine on one CI runner against an internal test service, to BlazeMeter. What is the best advice?
options: Move it; cloud is always better
Keep it local or in CI; BlazeMeter adds most value for scale, geography and shared reporting the team does not need here, and the target is internal
questions.explanation: Small loads against internal services fit local or CI runs. Cloud adds cost and needs reachability (or a private location) without solving a real problem here.
